guides.title: The 4-month sleep regression: why it happens and how to get through it
guides.description: Why baby sleep seems to fall apart around 4 months, what's actually happening in the brain, how long it lasts, and what helps — no magic promises, grounded in research.

faq.question: Is the 4-month sleep regression really a regression?
faq.answer: Technically, no. The word stuck in popular culture, but what's happening is a permanent shift in sleep architecture — the baby moves to adult-like sleep cycles with lighter stages in the middle. Pediatric sleep researchers usually call it a 'progression' or maturation. The feeling of things getting worse is real for parents, but it's a sign of development, not a step backward.

faq.question: How long does this phase usually last?
faq.answer: For most babies, between 2 and 6 weeks. There's no fixed timeline — some reorganize sleep in a few days, others take more than a month. What changes permanently is the structure of sleep itself; what slowly improves is the baby's ability to navigate the new cycle transitions without full assistance.

faq.question: Can I sleep-train at this age?
faq.answer: It's a family decision, and there's no scientific consensus telling you to do it or to avoid it. The AAP recognizes that several approaches (extinction, graduated extinction, fading) have evidence of effectiveness from 4–6 months of age, and that gentler strategies also work well for many families. The key is choosing what fits your family's values, your baby's temperament, and the caregivers' mental health. Talk it through with your pediatrician before deciding.

faq.question: Can I 'prevent' the regression?
faq.answer: No. The neurological maturation will happen no matter what you do. What can help is building, before or during the phase, conditions that ease the reorganization: a dark sleep environment at night, a predictable bedtime routine, and learning to tell brief physiological wakings (which often resolve on their own) from wakings driven by hunger or discomfort.

faq.question: Does feeding more before bed help the baby sleep longer?
faq.answer: There's no solid evidence of this for 4-month-olds. Studies don't show that extra feeds at night, early solids, or cereal in a bottle improve sleep — and introducing solids before 6 months carries its own risks. Real hunger exists and should be met, but 'loading up' on food as a sleep strategy doesn't hold up in most studies.

faq.question: When should I call the pediatrician?
faq.answer: Seek evaluation if there's weight loss, persistent feeding refusal, fever, inconsolable crying that's changed in pattern, signs of pain when swallowing or lying down, loud snoring or breathing pauses during sleep — or if you (the caregiver) are in significant mental distress. A few weeks of fragmented sleep without other symptoms is expected at this age; caregiver exhaustion that's putting safe care at risk is not.

guides.title: Baby Always Wants to Be Held: Is It Normal? When to Worry
guides.description: Baby cries when you put them down and only wants to be held? What to expect at each age, whether holding spoils a baby, how to free your hands, and when to call.

faq.question: Is it normal for a baby to only want to be held?
faq.answer: Most of the time, yes. In the first months, crying is at its highest and holding is one of the ways to calm it. Later, around 9 months, separation anxiety gets stronger and your baby may protest when you step away. See your pediatrician if it comes with fever, pain, refusing to feed, inconsolable crying or a sudden change in behavior.

faq.question: Does holding a baby too much spoil them?
faq.answer: There is no evidence that holding spoils a baby. In a clinical trial of 99 healthy mother-infant pairs, more time held during the day reduced crying by 43% at 6 weeks, with no change in sleep. From 4 months, the American Academy of Pediatrics notes that babies always rocked to sleep may have more trouble getting back to sleep at night, and that can change if it is weighing on the family.

faq.question: Until what age are babies clingy?
faq.answer: It varies. The American Academy of Pediatrics describes separation anxiety as possibly appearing at 4 or 5 months, getting stronger around 9 months, usually peaking between 10 and 18 months and fading in the second half of the second year. If your child gets very distressed by any separation or seems sad or anxious, talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: My baby only stops crying when held upright. Could it be reflux?
faq.answer: It could, among other causes. Many babies prefer being upright simply because they like the position and movement. Tell your pediatrician if your baby also arches their body, seems to be in pain, vomits often, refuses to feed or isn't gaining weight. You can't conclude this at home, and any treatment should only be with guidance from your pediatrician.

faq.question: What do I do when my baby only wants to be held and I need my hands?
faq.answer: Try a sling or carrier, with their face visible and chin off the chest. Take turns with another adult and give floor time with you nearby. If your baby is safe and you are at your limit, you can put them on their back in the crib and leave for a few minutes. Never shake a baby.

guides.title: Baby fever: when to worry and when to call the pediatrician
guides.description: What counts as a fever, how to measure it right, the age rule (why under 3 months is an emergency), when to seek help, how to ease it safely at home, and the myths you can drop.

faq.question: What temperature counts as a fever in a baby?
faq.answer: A fever is a rectal temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher — the most reliable reading in babies. Under the arm, readings from about 99.5–100°F (37.5–37.8°C) deserve attention, but the armpit tends to underestimate. The number alone matters less than your baby's age and how they're behaving.

faq.question: My baby is under 3 months and has a fever. What do I do?
faq.answer: Seek medical care right away, even if they seem fine. In babies under 3 months, a fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher is always an emergency: the immune system is still immature and serious infections can progress fast and without other signs. Don't give any medicine on your own before they're evaluated, so you don't mask the picture.

faq.question: Can I give medicine to bring the fever down?
faq.answer: Only with your pediatrician's guidance. This guide does not recommend medicines or doses: which medicine, whether it's needed and how much depend on your baby's age, weight and medical evaluation. Under 3 months, never medicate before they're evaluated. And remember: the goal is your baby's comfort, not 'zeroing' the thermometer — fluids and light clothing are part of the care.

faq.question: Does a high fever cause brain damage or seizures?
faq.answer: The common fever of infections (which rarely tops 104.9°F / 40.5°C) does not cause brain damage. It can trigger a febrile seizure in some children aged 6 months to 5 years — frightening, but almost always benign and without lasting effects. Brain damage only occurs with extreme hyperthermia (above ~107.6°F / 42°C), typical of heatstroke, not infection.

faq.question: Can I give a cold bath or rub alcohol to bring the fever down?
faq.answer: No. Cold baths, ice packs, and rubbing alcohol on the skin are contraindicated: they cause shivering (which raises temperature), discomfort, and — with alcohol — poisoning through the skin. A lukewarm (not cold) bath can be soothing if your baby likes it. Focus on hydration, light clothing, and easing the discomfort.

faq.question: Does teething cause a fever?
faq.answer: Teething can cause a slight rise in temperature (usually below 100.4°F / 38°C), irritability, and drooling — but it does NOT cause a high fever. If your baby is at 100.4°F (38°C) or above, don't blame teething: look for another cause and, when in doubt, see the pediatrician.

guides.title: Baby's first-year vaccine schedule (CDC + WHO overview)
guides.description: Which vaccines your baby gets from birth to 12 months under the US CDC/ACIP schedule, what each one protects against, expected side effects, red flags, and what to do if you fall behind. Evidence-based guide for new parents.

faq.question: Can I vaccinate my baby with a mild cold?
faq.answer: Yes. Mild colds, runny nose and slight cough — without fever or a clearly unwell baby — do NOT contraindicate vaccination. The only universal contraindication is a moderate to severe acute illness with fever; in that case, postpone the dose for a few days. A previous severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to that vaccine or one of its components also contraindicates further doses of that immunizer.

faq.question: Is fever after a vaccine normal?
faq.answer: Yes — low to moderate fever (up to 39°C / 102°F) in the first 24–48 hours is an expected reaction, a sign that the immune system is responding. If there's actual fever or discomfort, ask your pediatrician what to do — don't medicate on your own. The CDC and AAP do NOT recommend 'preventive' medicine before or right after the vaccine, because it may blunt the immune response.

faq.question: If I fall behind on a dose, do I have to start all over?
faq.answer: No. The schedule is cumulative: doses already given still count. You don't need to restart any series — just complete the missing doses as soon as possible. Visit your pediatrician with the immunization record, and they will calculate the catch-up schedule (the CDC publishes a specific catch-up table).

faq.question: Do vaccines cause autism?
faq.answer: No. The 1998 study suggesting that link was retracted by The Lancet for fraud, and its author lost his medical license. Since then, more than a dozen large studies (including a 2019 Danish study with 657,000 children) have confirmed that there is NO relationship between vaccination and autism. Vaccine hesitancy is one of the top global health threats listed by the WHO.

faq.question: When is my baby actually protected after a shot?
faq.answer: It depends on the vaccine. Most protections start to develop 1–2 weeks after the dose, but it's the complete schedule (usually 3 primary doses in the first year plus boosters) that creates lasting immunity. That's why following the schedule on time matters.

faq.question: How does the WHO schedule differ from the CDC?
faq.answer: WHO publishes a recommended global routine immunization schedule that includes BCG (tuberculosis) at birth and uses a 6/10/14-week pattern in many countries. The CDC schedule (US) skips BCG (low US TB burden) and uses 2/4/6 months. Both protect against the same priority diseases (DTaP, polio, Hib, pneumococcus, rotavirus, hepatitis B, MMR). If you live or travel outside the US, follow your country's national schedule.

guides.title: Baby Growth Charts: How to Read Weight, Length and Percentiles
guides.description: How to read your baby's growth chart (WHO standards): what a percentile means, how much weight babies gain per month, why the 3rd percentile can be as healthy as the 97th, and which curve changes deserve attention.

faq.question: What does my baby's percentile mean?
faq.answer: The percentile compares your baby with the WHO reference for the same age and sex: being at the 25th percentile for weight means that, out of 100 healthy babies, about 25 weigh less and 75 weigh more. It's not a grade or a ranking: the 3rd and the 97th can be equally healthy. What the pediatrician assesses isn't the isolated number, but whether the baby follows their OWN growth channel across visits. (In Brazil's Child Health Booklet the same curve also appears as z-scores — formal diagnoses use the -2 and -3 standard-deviation cutoffs; percentile and z-score are two rulers for the same map.)

faq.question: How much weight does a baby gain per month?
faq.answer: As a practical clinic rule (the WHO publishes detailed velocity tables, with wide dispersion): month 1 is the most intense (median above 800 g); from 1 to 3 months, about 700 to 900 g per month (20 to 30 g/day); 3 to 6 months, 450 to 600 g per month; 6 to 9 months, 300 to 450 g; 9 to 12 months, 200 to 400 g. The slowdown through the year is expected and healthy. Remember the physiological loss of the first week (above ~7% usually prompts a closer look at feeding, and above 10%, further evaluation without delay), typically regained between days 10 and 14 — and daily gain counts from the lowest point.

faq.question: My baby is in the 10th percentile. Should I worry?
faq.answer: A stable low percentile is usually just that baby's size — genetics counts a lot, especially after 6 months (before that, the intrauterine environment weighs more). What deserves investigation isn't being at the 10th, but crossing percentile lines downward in a sustained way, stopping weight gain, or weight detaching from length. The one who separates normal variation (including the physiological catch-up/catch-down adjustments between 6 and 24 months) from a problem is the pediatrician, with the full curve in hand.

faq.question: Do formula-fed babies grow differently from breastfed ones?
faq.answer: The WHO standards were built with breastfed babies — that's the growth considered ideal. Observational studies show formula-fed babies tend, on average, to gain weight somewhat faster in the second half of the year — a group tendency, not an individual rule — which reinforces responsive feeding (respecting fullness) so the tendency doesn't become excess. The reference curve used is the same for everyone.

faq.question: How often should I weigh and measure my baby?
faq.answer: At routine checkups. Weighing at home every week (or every day) creates more anxiety than information: daily fluctuations from diapers, feeds and different scales deceive. The months-long trend is what matters — different scales on different days aren't comparable. The real exception: when the pediatrician asks for more frequent weight checks (a newborn struggling to gain, for example) — then it's with their guidance, technique and scale.

faq.question: What about premature babies?
faq.answer: Preterm babies get their own reading: plotting chronological age on the standard curve creates false alarms. Corrected age (discounting the weeks missing to 40) is used on the WHO curves — generally until age 2 — and, in the neonatal period, preterm-specific curves (like Intergrowth-21st or Fenton), depending on the service. If your baby was born early, always ask which age and which curve are being used.

guides.title: Developmental milestones at 12 months: what to expect
guides.description: What a 1-year-old typically does — pulling to stand, cruising, first words, gestures, the pincer grasp — by area, the feeding changes at 1 year, how to encourage development, and when to talk to the pediatrician.

faq.question: What does a 1-year-old typically do?
faq.answer: Around 12 months, many babies pull up to stand on furniture, walk holding on (cruising), pick up small objects with the pincer grasp (thumb and index finger), put things into a container, wave bye-bye, call a parent by a special name, and understand 'no.' It's a wide range: every baby has their own pace.

faq.question: Does a 12-month-old have to walk?
faq.answer: No. At 12 months, what's expected is pulling to stand and walking holding on to furniture ('cruising'). Walking on their own has a wide window — many babies walk between 12 and 15 months, and walking only later, up to around 18 months, is still normal. What deserves attention is NOT being able to stand with support at 12 months.

faq.question: My 1-year-old isn't talking yet. Is that normal?
faq.answer: It can be. At 12 months, many babies say 1 to 3 little words besides 'mama/dada,' but there's a lot of variation. Just as important as words are gestures: waving bye-bye, pointing, shaking the head. If at 12 months the baby makes no gestures, doesn't point, and doesn't respond to their name or to 'no,' mention it to the pediatrician.

faq.question: When should I worry about development at 12 months?
faq.answer: Talk to the pediatrician if the baby doesn't move around in any way (no crawling, scooting, or cruising), doesn't stand when supported, doesn't look for objects they saw you hide, doesn't say any little word like 'mama/dada,' doesn't learn gestures (waving, head shaking), doesn't point, or has lost skills they once had. Losing skills is always a reason to look into it.

faq.question: Do milestones apply to premature babies?
faq.answer: For babies born prematurely, use corrected age (subtracting the weeks of prematurity) for the first 2 years. A baby born 2 months early is assessed as if 10 months old when they turn 12 months. That's expected, and the pediatrician follows it.

faq.question: Can I give cow's milk to my 1-year-old?
faq.answer: Yes. From age 1, whole cow's milk can be part of the diet (before that, it's not recommended as the main drink). Breastfeeding can continue as long as the family wishes. It's also the stage to gradually swap the bottle for a cup and offer more family food, always with your pediatrician's guidance.

guides.title: Developmental milestones at 6 months: what to expect
guides.description: What a 6-month-old typically does — sitting with support, rolling, babbling, grabbing objects — by developmental area, the signs of readiness for solids, how to encourage development, and when to talk to the pediatrician.

faq.question: What does a 6-month-old typically do?
faq.answer: Around 6 months, many babies roll (at least one way), push up with straight arms on their tummy, sit with support, bring objects and their own feet to their mouth, grab toys, babble and blow 'raspberries' (a motor sound with the tongue), laugh, and recognize familiar faces. It's a wide range: every baby has their own pace.

faq.question: Does a 6-month-old sit on their own?
faq.answer: At 6 months, many babies sit with support or start the 'tripod sit' (hands propped on the floor in front). Sitting fully without support usually comes a bit later — generally between 6 and 9 months. It's normal variation; what matters is the progress over the weeks.

faq.question: My 6-month-old isn't rolling yet. Is that normal?
faq.answer: It can be. Rolling appears across a wide range, and some babies roll a little later. Look at the whole picture: if they have good head control, push up on their arms when on their tummy, and reach for objects, they're probably on track. But unlike crawling (which some babies skip), a complete absence of rolling deserves attention: if by 6 months they don't roll at all in any direction, mention it to the pediatrician.

faq.question: When should I worry about development at 6 months?
faq.answer: Talk to the pediatrician if the baby doesn't try to reach for objects, doesn't bring things to their mouth, doesn't react to sounds around them, shows no affection for caregivers, doesn't babble or squeal, doesn't roll in any direction, or seems very stiff or very floppy. The earlier it's looked into, the better.

faq.question: Do milestones apply to premature babies?
faq.answer: For babies born prematurely, use corrected age (subtracting the weeks of prematurity) for the first 2 years. A baby born 2 months early, for example, is assessed as if 4 months old at 6 months of life. That's expected, and the pediatrician follows it.

faq.question: Can my 6-month-old start eating?
faq.answer: Around 6 months, most babies show signs of readiness: good head control, sitting with support, showing interest in food, and no longer pushing everything out with the tongue. Starting solids goes slowly, always keeping milk (breast milk or formula) as the main food until age 1. Confirm the timing with your pediatrician.

guides.description: 0–3 months: 3 to 5 naps; 3–6 months: 3 to 4; 6–9: 2 to 3; 9–12: 2; from 12 to 18 months down to 1. Nap length by age, best times and when to drop a nap.

faq.question: Should I wake the baby from a nap so it doesn't ruin the night?
faq.answer: It depends on age and timing. Before 4 months, rarely worth waking — day and night sleep are still consolidating together. From 4-6 months onward, consider waking if: 1) the nap has gone past 2 hours uninterrupted, or 2) the baby is sleeping too close to bedtime (ideally, end the last nap at least 2-4 hours before night sleep starts — varies with age). Wake gently: light, voice, diaper change — never shaking.

faq.question: Is a short 30-45 minute nap a problem?
faq.answer: Before 4-6 months, no — that's the size of one infant sleep cycle (30-50 min), and waking between cycles is physiological. After that, chronic 30-minute naps with the baby waking exhausted may signal environment (too much light, noise), overtiredness, hunger, or a poorly timed wake window. If it's occasional, it's normal. If it's the pattern for 2+ weeks, worth adjusting.

faq.question: Baby only sleeps in arms, sling, or stroller. Is that a problem?
faq.answer: In the first trimester it's totally normal and even desirable (skin-to-skin regulates the baby). From 3-4 months on, as the baby can self-soothe more, start offering naps in the crib without pressure. There's no rigid deadline. For naps in arms, the adult needs to stay awake and alert, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises moving the baby to a firm, flat surface as soon as possible; naps on soft surfaces (sofa, armchair) with an adult sleeping is a major SIDS risk.

faq.question: When do I drop the morning nap?
faq.answer: Typically between 12 and 18 months — the morning nap is almost always the first to go (the afternoon nap stays). Signs it's time: repeated refusal of the morning nap for 1-2 weeks, the morning nap pushing the afternoon one too late, or bedtime resistance. When you drop it, expect a 2-4 week transition where the baby may be tired at an odd time — bringing the single nap forward by 30-60 min often helps.

faq.question: Do naps have to be in the dark?
faq.answer: No, and before 4 months it can actually hinder. Melatonin levels are naturally low during the day — darkening the room doesn't 'turn on' production, just removes visual stimulation. In the first trimester, naps with some natural light help the baby establish the circadian rhythm and distinguish day from night. From 4-6 months on, more sensitive babies tend to nap better in a darkened room — but soft dimness (regular curtain, low light) is usually enough. Full blackout is rarely needed.

faq.question: How do I know naps are working?
faq.answer: Three practical indicators. 1) The baby wakes from naps in a good mood (not crying immediately); 2) Handles the next wake window without becoming exhausted; 3) Night sleep falls within the expected range for their age. If any of these consistently fails, review timing, total duration, and environment. A baby with age-appropriate total nap time almost always sleeps better at night, not worse.

faq.question: Is it normal for a baby to only sleep when held?
faq.answer: Yes, it is very common, especially in the first months. The NHS in the UK describes it as common for babies to fall asleep while held and wake when put in the cot. Before 4 months there is no rush to change anything. Around that age you can start gradually, if holding is becoming too much for the family.

faq.question: How long should I wait before putting my baby in the crib after they fall asleep?
faq.answer: A Japanese study of 21 babies suggests about 5 to 8 minutes after they fall asleep. Babies put down sooner woke more often. The study is small and its authors ask for confirmation, so use this as a starting point. If you feel sleepy during that wait, put your baby in the crib right away.

faq.question: Will holding my baby too much spoil them?
faq.answer: Holding does not spoil a baby, and in the first months contact helps calm them. What the American Academy of Pediatrics notes, for babies 4 months and older, is that those who are always rocked to sleep may have more trouble getting back to sleep when they wake at night. That is a sleep habit, and it can change whenever the family wants.

faq.question: At what age can I teach my baby to sleep in the crib?
faq.answer: The American Academy of Pediatrics suggests putting babies in the crib drowsy from 4 months. More structured methods, such as gradually waiting longer before responding, have been studied in older babies, from 6 months. One review found no proven benefit from these methods before 6 months. Talk to your pediatrician before starting.

faq.question: What if my baby falls asleep in a sling or in my arms during the day?
faq.answer: It happens, and the adult needs to stay awake and attentive. In a sling, their face needs to stay visible, with the chin off the chest. Arms and slings are not a regular place to sleep: the American Academy of Pediatrics advises moving them to a firm, flat surface, on their back, as soon as possible. The biggest risk comes when the adult falls asleep too, especially on a sofa or armchair.

guides.title: Baby reflux: what's normal, how to manage it, and when it's a disease
guides.description: The difference between normal reflux (spitting up) and reflux disease, why most babies spit up, what actually helps at home, why medication is rarely needed, and the warning signs that call for the pediatrician.

faq.question: Is spitting up normal? My baby spits up after almost every feed.
faq.answer: Yes, it's very normal. Reflux (spitting up) happens because the valve between the stomach and esophagus is still immature and relaxes easily. More than half of babies spit up in the first months, peaking around 4 months. If your baby gains weight, is comfortable, and has no warning signs, it's physiological reflux — a laundry problem, not a health one. It usually improves on its own by 12 months.

faq.question: What's the difference between reflux and reflux disease (GERD)?
faq.answer: Reflux (GER) is the stomach contents coming back up the esophagus — common and normal in babies. It becomes reflux disease (GERD) when it causes complications: poor weight gain, feeding refusal, significant pain, bleeding, or breathing problems. Most babies who spit up do NOT have GERD — they're 'happy spitters,' who spit up but keep thriving.

faq.question: Does my baby need medication for reflux?
faq.answer: In most cases, no. Acid-reducing medicines don't help physiological reflux and can carry risks — they're reserved for GERD confirmed by the pediatrician. For a baby who spits up but is well, the treatment is reassuring the parents and adjusting the feeding routine, not medicating.

faq.question: Can I raise the head of the crib or lay my baby on their side because of reflux?
faq.answer: No. Even with reflux, your baby should ALWAYS sleep on their back, on a firm, flat surface, without raising the head of the crib or using positioners — those practices raise the risk of sudden infant death and don't reduce reflux during sleep. Holding your baby upright helps while they're awake, not while sleeping.

faq.question: Could the reflux be a cow's milk allergy?
faq.answer: In some cases, yes. Cow's milk protein allergy can cause symptoms that look like GERD (irritability, vomiting, sometimes blood in the stool or a rash). If that's suspected, the pediatrician may suggest an elimination trial — in the breastfeeding mother's diet or by switching the formula. Don't make restrictions on your own; it's a medical decision.

faq.question: When does baby reflux usually go away?
faq.answer: Physiological reflux improves as the baby matures, sits up, and spends more time upright. Most cases resolve between 6 and 12 months, and nearly all by 12–18 months. If it persists well beyond that, gets worse, or comes with warning signs, see the pediatrician.

guides.title: Baby Refuses Solids, Only Wants to Breastfeed: What to Do
guides.description: Baby 6 to 12 months refuses solids, only wants to breastfeed? Why it happens, how to time nursing and meals, what to avoid, when to see the pediatrician.

faq.question: My baby only wants the breast and refuses food. Is that normal?
faq.answer: It's common, especially in the first months of solids. The breast is easy and familiar and also gives comfort, while eating takes work. In most cases it improves with routine, time and less pressure. See the pediatrician if the refusal is total for two weeks or more, if weight stops going up, or if there's pain, vomiting or coughing when eating.

faq.question: Should I breastfeed before or after solids?
faq.answer: When you can, offer food first and the breast after, and avoid nursing right before a meal. A baby with a full stomach has little reason to accept food. We found no study comparing the two orders at this age, and the guidance varies: the UK's NHS recommends milk after food, and Brazil's Ministry of Health says the breast can be offered whenever the baby wants. What changes is the timing. You don't need to cut the number of feeds on your own.

faq.question: Do I need to stop breastfeeding for my baby to eat?
faq.answer: No. The WHO recommends continuing to breastfeed to 2 years or beyond, alongside food, and breast milk remains the main source of energy and nutrients before 1 year. If you want to wean for another reason, that's a family decision, but cutting out the breast to force acceptance can take away calories your baby isn't yet replacing with food. Talk to the pediatrician first.

faq.question: My baby cries at the sight of food. Should I keep trying?
faq.answer: No. If your baby cries and asks for the breast, end the meal without a fight, nurse, and offer food again at the next mealtime. Forcing, fighting or bribing tends to make their relationship with food worse. If your baby gags at the mere sight of food, or if the refusal started suddenly after choking or a scare, tell the pediatrician.

faq.question: How much should a 9-month-old eat?
faq.answer: The dietary guide from Brazil's Ministry of Health gives about 4 to 5 tablespoons in total at each main meal, from 9 to 11 months, as a reference, and warns that this number shouldn't be followed rigidly. The best way to know if your baby is eating enough is to track weight and length on the growth chart with the pediatrician.

guides.title: Baby's Room: Temperature, Fans and Safe Sleep
guides.description: What is the right temperature for a baby's room? Fans, air conditioning, humidifiers, light, white noise, tummy sleeping and raised cribs: what the sources say.

faq.question: What is the ideal temperature for a baby's room?
faq.answer: The UK's NHS gives 16 to 20 °C. The American Academy of Pediatrics gives no number, and that range is hard to keep in hot climates. On hot days, what helps most is ventilating the room, using little clothing, skipping blankets and checking that your baby isn't sweaty or hot on the chest.

faq.question: Can I leave a fan on in the baby's room?
faq.answer: Guidance varies. An American study linked fan use with a lower risk of sudden infant death, but it doesn't prove cause, and a leaflet from a British health service advises not leaving a fan in the room while the baby sleeps. Since the sources disagree, the simplest option is to cool the room before your baby sleeps. If the family decides to use one, don't aim it at your baby and keep the cord and device out of reach.

faq.question: Can a baby sleep on their stomach?
faq.answer: No. Babies should be placed on their back for every sleep until age 1, and the American Academy of Pediatrics considers the side position just as dangerous as the stomach. If your baby already rolls easily both ways, you don't need to turn them back during the night.

faq.question: Can I raise the crib for reflux or a stuffy nose?
faq.answer: No. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that babies sleep on a flat surface, including with reflux, and considers any incline above 10 degrees unsafe. Wedges, towels and pillows under the baby or the mattress are not safe.

faq.question: Is a humidifier good for a baby?
faq.answer: It can help with a stuffy nose, and the American Academy of Pediatrics mentions a cool mist humidifier, out of the baby's reach. Change the water every day and follow the manufacturer's cleaning instructions. Avoid hot steam models, which can cause burns. Mold and bacteria are the problem with a dirty device.

guides.title: 10-Month-Old Sleep Schedule: Wake Windows of 3h15 to 4h
guides.description: At 10 months, wake windows run 3h15 to 4h, with 2 naps and 12 to 15 hours of sleep a day. A flexible schedule, early-morning waking and the baby who stands in the crib.

faq.question: How much does a 10-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: The recommendation is 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps; observational studies show many babies closer to 13 hours. Night holds most of it, in one long stretch, and the day splits into 2 naps. The range of normal is wide — and sleep is just one signal: weigh it together with feeding, weight gain and energy, and bring questions to the routine check-up.

faq.question: Can a 10-month-old switch to just 1 nap?
faq.answer: Almost always not yet. The transition to 1 nap usually happens between 12 and 18 months. At 10 months, refusing a nap is usually a phase (motor practice, separation) — not a sign of too much sleep. Dropping a nap too early tends to make nights worse and the morning wake-up even earlier.

faq.question: My 10-month-old wakes at 5 a.m. What can I do?
faq.answer: Very early waking usually has stacked causes: going to bed overtired (too much tiredness fragments the end of the night), naps that ran too short, a room that brightens early, or a bedtime that drifted too early or too late. Before changing everything, check the wake windows and truly darken the room. Small, consistent adjustments held for several days work better than big swings.

faq.question: My baby stands in the crib and won't lie down. How do I handle it?
faq.answer: It's classic for 9 to 11 months: the skill is new and your baby wants to practice. During the day, rehearse standing up and sitting back down a lot (outside the crib). At night, lay them back down calmly, few words, low light — without turning it into a game or a battle. The phase passes once the novelty wears off. And check that the crib mattress is already on its lowest setting.

faq.question: Does a 10-month-old still need night feeds?
faq.answer: Many 10-month-olds with good weight gain already go through the night without feeding, while others still wake 1 to 2 times — also common, especially with breastfeeding. The real need depends on each baby's growth and history (preemies and babies with slow weight gain are a separate case). If you want to actively reduce night feeds, align the plan with your pediatrician.

guides.description: At 11 months, wake windows run 3h30 to 4h, with 2 naps and 12 to 15 hours of sleep a day. A flexible schedule, first steps shaking up nights and the real transition to 1 nap.

faq.question: How much does an 11-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: The National Sleep Foundation recommends 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps (the AASM works with 12 to 16); observational studies show many babies closer to 13 hours. Night holds most of it, in one long stretch, and the day splits into 2 naps. The range of normal is wide — weigh sleep together with feeding, weight gain and energy, and bring questions to the routine check-up.

faq.question: My 11-month-old is refusing a nap: is this the transition to 1 nap?
faq.answer: Most of the time, not yet. The real transition usually happens between 12 and 18 months (for many babies only around 14–16 months) and gives consistent signs for 2 weeks or more: the morning nap shortens or keeps drifting later every day, the afternoon one stays solid, and nights stay good. Three bad days in a motor-leap week aren't a sign — they're a phase. When in doubt, protect the 2 naps.

faq.question: Do first steps disturb sleep?
faq.answer: They often do — temporarily. Big motor milestones (standing alone, first steps) come with an intense urge to practice, crib included, and can bring extra wakings or nap resistance for a few days to a few weeks. Lots of walking practice during the day and a predictable routine help the phase pass without creating new habits.

faq.question: My 11-month-old still wakes at night. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes. Many 11-month-olds get through the night without feeding, and others still wake — in observational studies of this age range, the average runs from under 1 up to about 2–3 signaled wakings per night, with breastfed babies feeding more often. The need for night feeds depends on each baby's growth and history; to reduce them actively, align the plan with your pediatrician.

faq.question: Can I add a pillow or blanket to the crib near the first birthday?
faq.answer: Not yet. Safe-sleep guidance covers the whole first year: a bare crib (no pillows, cushions, bumpers, loose blankets or large toys), baby placed on their back, and a sleep sack for warmth. Pillow and blanket come much later, at the transition to a bed — not in an 11-month-old's crib.

faq.question: How much does a 1-year-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: At 12 months the recommendation changes bands: the National Sleep Foundation indicates 11 to 14 hours a day for ages 1–2 (the AASM also works with 11 to 14), counting night and naps. Night holds 10 to 12 hours and the day still splits, for most, into 2 naps. As always, weigh sleep together with feeding, weight gain and energy.

faq.question: Does a 1-year-old switch to just 1 nap?
faq.answer: Most not yet. The transition window opens now (12 to 18 months), but many babies only consolidate 1 nap around 14 to 16 months. The sign of a real transition is consistency for 2 weeks or more — the morning nap shortening or drifting later every day with nights staying good. Three bad days in a week of party, tooth or virus don't count.

faq.question: Can I give cow's milk in the bedtime bottle at 1 year?
faq.answer: From 12 months whole cow's milk is usually cleared by the pediatrician, but two cautions apply at night: milk sitting on teeth during sleep is one of the main factors in early childhood caries (brush after the last milk), and a bottle at sleep onset becomes a sleep association that's hard to undo. The general guidance is to discourage bottles in the crib and plan bottle weaning across the second year, with your pediatrician.

faq.question: My 1-year-old still wakes overnight. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes. In observational studies of this age range, signaled wakings remain common — from under 1 up to about 2 per night (sometimes more), with breastfed babies feeding more often. What weighs in now: separation anxiety (usually at its height), molars arriving and walking practice. The need for night feeds depends on each baby's growth and history — to reduce them, align with your pediatrician.

faq.question: When can I add a pillow and blanket to the crib?
faq.answer: Not yet. Sudden infant death syndrome is, by definition, a first-year risk — after the birthday what remains are suffocation, strangulation and fall risks, which is why the practical guidance is still a bare crib while your child sleeps in one. Pillow and blanket come with the transition to a bed (usually between 18 months and 3 years). What changes now: a lovey (a small transitional object) becomes acceptable in the crib from 12 months.

guides.description: At 2 months, babies stay awake 60 to 90 minutes between sleeps, take 4 to 5 naps and sleep 14 to 17 hours a day. A flexible schedule and what's normal to expect.

faq.question: How much does a 2-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually between 14 and 17 hours a day, counting night sleep and naps — with normal variation between babies. Sleep is still spread across the 24 hours, in several blocks. If your baby sleeps a bit more or a bit less and is active, feeding, and gaining weight, it's probably fine.

faq.question: How many naps does a 2-month-old take?
faq.answer: Usually 4 to 5 naps a day, of variable length (some 30–45 minutes, others longer). Short naps are common and normal at this age — sleep is still maturing. Don't expect fixed times: at 2 months, the rhythm is still very flexible.

faq.question: Does a 2-month-old sleep through the night?
faq.answer: No, and that's normal. At 2 months your baby still wakes to feed at night. Some start doing a longer block (4 to 6 hours), but sleeping all night without waking isn't expected at this stage. Night feeds still matter for growth.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 2 months?
faq.answer: Around 60 to 90 minutes awake between one sleep and the next. Going much beyond that tends to leave the baby 'overtired' — fussier and harder to settle. Watching sleepy cues (yawning, glazed stare, going quiet or fussy) helps more than following the clock.

faq.question: My 2-month-old only sleeps in my arms. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes, very common. At this stage the baby still seeks contact to feel secure. You can start putting them in the crib drowsy but still awake so they get used to it — no pressure, and no sleep training, which isn't recommended this early. It's a gradual transition, not a rule.

faq.question: Can I let my 2-month-old sleep through the night without waking to feed?
faq.answer: Talk to your pediatrician. At 2 months, most babies still need night feeds, and many are still woken for them if they sleep too long, especially while weight gain is being monitored. Babies who sleep long blocks and gain weight well may have more flexibility — but that's individual and decided with the pediatrician.

faq.question: How much does a 3-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 14 to 17 hours a day, counting night sleep and naps, with the average edging toward 15 hours. Sleep starts to concentrate a bit more at night than at 2 months. There's normal variation between babies: if yours is active, feeding, and gaining weight, it's probably fine.

faq.question: How many naps does a 3-month-old take?
faq.answer: Usually 3 to 5 naps a day, still of variable length. They gradually start to organize, but fixed times aren't yet the rule at 3 months. Short naps remain common and normal at this stage.

faq.question: Does a 3-month-old sleep through the night?
faq.answer: Some 3-month-olds do a longer night block (5 to 6 hours or more), but sleeping all night without waking still isn't the rule. Most keep waking 1 to 3 times to feed. It's a wide range of normal — comparing with other babies only breeds anxiety.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 3 months?
faq.answer: Around 75 to 105 minutes (about 1h15 to 1h45) awake between one sleep and the next — a bit more than at 2 months. Going much beyond that tends to leave the baby 'overtired.' Watching sleepy cues still matters more than following the clock.

faq.question: Can I start a sleep routine at 3 months?
faq.answer: A light, flexible routine, yes — like a calm wind-down before sleep (bath, feed, dim room) and clearly distinguishing day from night. But rigid schedules and sleep training still aren't recommended at this age. Think rhythm and predictability, not the clock.

faq.question: My 3-month-old suddenly started waking more at night. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes, it can be normal. Near the end of the 3rd month and start of the 4th, many babies go through the 4-month sleep regression — a real change in how they sleep that tends to disrupt nights for a few weeks. It's a sign of maturing, not going backward, and it passes.

guides.description: At 4 months, wake windows run 1h30 to 2h, with 3 to 4 naps and 12 to 16 hours of sleep a day. A flexible schedule, night sleep and what to expect at this age.

faq.question: How much does a 4-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 16 hours a day counting night and naps, with the average around 14 to 15 hours. There's a wide range of normal: if your baby is active, feeding well and gaining weight, things are probably fine even if they sleep a little more or a little less than average.

faq.question: What is the 4-month sleep regression?
faq.answer: It's a permanent change in how your baby sleeps: around 4 months sleep matures into adult-like cycles with brief awakenings between them. The baby who used to 'crash out' now wakes lightly at the end of each cycle and has to relearn how to fall back asleep. That's why nights get worse for a few weeks. Despite the name, it's a developmental step forward, not a step back.

faq.question: Does a 4-month-old sleep through the night?
faq.answer: Some 4-month-olds already do a longer stretch early in the night, but sleeping all the way through without waking isn't the rule yet: most wake 1 to 2 times to feed, and that's normal and expected at this age. With the 4-month regression, it's common to have even more wakings for a few weeks.

faq.question: How many naps does a 4-month-old take?
faq.answer: Typically 3 to 4 naps a day. They start settling into slightly more predictable times but still vary in length. Short 30- to 45-minute naps stay common at this stage, partly because of the sleep maturation itself.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 4 months?
faq.answer: Around 90 to 120 minutes (1.5 to 2 hours) awake between sleeps, sometimes closer to 2h15 by the end of the day. Going much beyond that tends to leave the baby overtired and, paradoxically, harder to settle. Watching sleepy cues still beats watching the clock.

faq.question: Do I need to stop swaddling at 4 months?
faq.answer: Yes — stop swaddling at the first sign your baby is trying to roll. That often shows up around 4 months, but it can start as early as 2 to 3 months, so don't wait for a set age or for them to actually roll. A swaddled baby who flips onto their tummy can't reposition and is at risk of suffocation. Keep placing them on their back, now with arms free.

faq.question: How much does a 5-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps, with the average around 14 hours. Sleep is now more concentrated at night than in earlier months. If your baby is active, feeding well and gaining weight, things are probably fine, even sleeping a little more or less than average.

faq.question: How many naps does a 5-month-old take?
faq.answer: Typically 3 naps a day, though some babies still take 4. They start settling into slightly more predictable times and some get longer, but short 30- to 45-minute naps are still common. The transition to 2 naps usually comes later, between 6 and 9 months.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 5 months?
faq.answer: Around 2 to 2.5 hours awake between sleeps — a bit longer than at 4 months. The last window of the day is usually the longest. Going much beyond that leaves the baby overtired and harder to settle. Watching sleepy cues still beats watching the clock.

faq.question: Does a 5-month-old sleep through the night?
faq.answer: Many 5-month-olds already do a longer stretch early in the night, but sleeping all the way through without waking isn't the rule yet. It's common to still have 0 to 2 wakings to feed, and breastfed babies tend to feed more often. All of that is normal at this age.

faq.question: My 5-month-old rolls and sleeps on their tummy. Is it safe?
faq.answer: If your baby can roll both ways on their own (back to tummy and back again), you can leave them in whatever position they choose — no need to keep flipping them all night. What matters is always placing them on their back to sleep, on a firm mattress with nothing loose in the crib. And even if they only roll one way, if they roll on their own during sleep there's no need to wake them to turn them back.

faq.question: Can I start solids at 5 months to help my baby sleep better?
faq.answer: Not for sleep's sake. The recommendation is to start solids around 6 months, when your baby shows signs of readiness. There's no solid evidence that offering purée or cereal earlier makes a baby sleep through the night, and starting solids early carries risks. Talk to your pediatrician about the right timing.

guides.description: At 6 months, wake windows run 2 to 3 hours, with 2 to 3 naps and 12 to 15 hours of sleep a day. A flexible schedule, night sleep and what to expect at this age.

faq.question: How much does a 6-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 15 hours a day, counting night sleep and naps, with the average around 14 hours. Most of the sleep now happens at night. There's normal variation between babies: if yours is active, eating, and growing well, it's probably fine.

faq.question: How many naps does a 6-month-old take?
faq.answer: Usually 2 to 3 naps a day. Somewhere between 6 and 9 months, many babies move from 3 to 2 longer, more predictable naps (one mid-morning and one early afternoon). It's a gradual transition — some days they still want a short third nap.

faq.question: Does a 6-month-old sleep through the night?
faq.answer: Many 6-month-olds do long night blocks, and some sleep through — but still waking 1 or 2 times is normal and common. Whether and when to drop night feeds is individual: talk to your pediatrician, especially if weight gain is going well.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 6 months?
faq.answer: Around 2 to 3 hours awake between one sleep and the next — much more than in the early months. The window is usually shorter in the morning and longer before night sleep. It's still worth watching sleepy cues, not just the clock.

faq.question: Can I start sleep training at 6 months?
faq.answer: From around 4 to 6 months, behavioral sleep methods become an option for families who want them — always gently and respecting the baby. It's not mandatory nor the only path to healthy sleep. It's a family choice, ideally discussed with your pediatrician.

faq.question: Can my 6-month-old sleep in their own room now?
faq.answer: Guidelines recommend room-sharing (baby in their own crib, in the parents' room) for at least the first 6 months. After that, moving to their own room is a family decision — what doesn't change are the safe-sleep rules.

faq.question: How much does a 7-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps, with the average around 14 hours. Most of it now happens at night, with a longer night stretch. If your baby is active, eating well and gaining weight, things are probably fine, even sleeping a little more or less than average.

faq.question: How many naps does a 7-month-old take?
faq.answer: Most take 2 to 3 naps a day. Seven months sits right in the middle of the 3-to-2 nap transition, which usually happens between 6 and 9 months. Some babies are already settled on 2 longer naps; others still need a short third nap in the late afternoon. Both are normal.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 7 months?
faq.answer: Around 2.5 to 3.5 hours awake between sleeps — much longer than in the early months. The last window of the day is usually the longest. If your baby is on 2 naps, windows are closer to 3 hours; on 3 naps, closer to 2.5.

faq.question: Why has my 7-month-old started waking more at night and crying when I leave?
faq.answer: It's probably separation anxiety, which usually shows up between 6 and 8 months. At this stage your baby understands you still exist out of sight (object permanence) but doesn't yet know you always come back — so they protest at being left, including at bedtime. It's a developmental milestone, not a setback, and it improves with predictability and patience.

faq.question: Can a 7-month-old sleep on their tummy?
faq.answer: If your baby already rolls and sits on their own, you can leave them in whatever position they choose during sleep — no need to keep flipping them all night. What matters is always placing them on their back to sleep, in a crib with a firm mattress and nothing loose (pillows, cushions, blankets). Once your baby can sit or push up on hands and knees (and even more so when they pull to stand), lower the crib mattress to its lowest level.

faq.question: How much does an 8-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps, with the average around 14 hours. Most of it now happens at night, in a long stretch, and daytime sleep is down to 2 naps for most babies. If your baby is active, eating well and gaining weight, things are probably fine.

faq.question: How many naps does an 8-month-old take?
faq.answer: Most are settled on 2 naps a day (morning and early afternoon), about 1 to 1.5 hours each. Some babies are still finishing the 3-to-2 nap transition, and that's fine. The move to 1 nap usually comes much later, between 12 and 18 months.

faq.question: What is the '8-month sleep regression'?
faq.answer: It's a rougher sleep patch that tends to show up between 8 and 10 months, but it's not really a regression: it's the combination of two developmental milestones — the peak of separation anxiety and big motor leaps (crawling, pulling to stand). The baby wakes more, resists naps and wants to 'practice' the new skills, even at night. It's temporary and passes with consistency.

faq.question: My baby stands up in the crib and cries without knowing how to lie down. What do I do?
faq.answer: It's very common at 8 months. During the day, teach and practice the sit-down/lie-down movement from standing, so they gain independence. At night, lay them down calmly and without turning it into a game; if they stand up again, repeat calmly. It usually resolves in one to two weeks, but it varies from baby to baby.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 8 months?
faq.answer: Around 2h45 to 3h45 awake between sleeps, with the last window of the day (before bed) being the longest. On 2 naps, windows are closer to 3 to 3.5 hours. Watching sleepy cues still beats watching the clock.

faq.question: How much does a 9-month-old sleep per day?
faq.answer: Usually about 12 to 15 hours a day counting night and naps, with the average around 14 hours. Most of it happens at night, in a long stretch, and the day splits into 2 naps. If your baby is active, eating well and gaining weight, things are probably fine, even sleeping a little more or less than average.

faq.question: My 9-month-old started refusing a nap. Is it time to move to 1 nap?
faq.answer: Almost certainly not. The move to 1 nap usually comes only between 12 and 18 months. At 9 months, nap refusals are usually a passing 'strike' tied to the developmental phase (separation, motor leaps) — not a sign of too much sleep. Dropping to 1 nap too early leaves the baby overtired and makes nights worse. Protect both naps and ride it out.

faq.question: What's the wake window (awake time) at 9 months?
faq.answer: Around 3 to 3h45 awake between sleeps, with the last window of the day (before bed) being the longest. Going much beyond that tends to leave the baby wound up and harder to settle. Watching sleepy cues still beats watching the clock.

faq.question: My 9-month-old still wakes at night. Is that normal?
faq.answer: Yes. Many 9-month-olds already sleep long stretches, but 0 to 2 wakings to feed are still within normal, and breastfed babies tend to feed more often. At this stage, wakings usually have more to do with development (separation, standing up) than with hunger. It's not the time to cut night feeds on your own.

faq.question: Is it safe for a 9-month-old to sleep on their tummy or sitting up?
faq.answer: If your baby already rolls, sits, and moves on their own, they can sleep in whatever position they choose — no need to keep flipping them all night. What matters is always laying them down on their back, with the crib mattress at its lowest level (they stand now) and the crib free of anything loose (pillows, cushions, blankets, large toys).

guides.description: How many times do babies wake at night at 3, 6, 8 and 12 months? Numbers from studies of thousands of babies, common causes, and when to call the pediatrician.

faq.question: How many times does a baby wake at night?
faq.answer: In two large Finnish studies, with parents reporting on about 1,000 to 2,000 babies at each age, the median was 2 wakings per night at 3, 6 and 8 months, 1.5 at 12 months and 1 at 18 and 24 months. There is a lot of variation: the common range at 6 months was 1 to 3.

faq.question: How many times does a 5-month-old wake at night?
faq.answer: The Finnish study did not measure 5 months, but at 3 and 6 months the median was 2 wakings per night, with a common range of 1.5 to 3 at 3 months and 1 to 3 at 6 months. A 5-month-old who wakes 1 to 3 times is within what is most frequent at these ages.

faq.question: At what age do babies sleep through the night?
faq.answer: There is no set age. In a Canadian study of 388 babies, between 27.9% and 57.0% were still not sleeping through the night at 6 and 12 months, depending on the criterion of 6 or 8 straight hours. Sleeping straight through was also not linked to better mental or motor development in that study.

faq.question: Is it normal for a baby to wake every hour?
faq.answer: It can happen in phases, such as during illness or changes in sleep, but it is not the most common pattern. At 8 months, 13.6% of babies needed help getting back to sleep 4 or more times a night in the Finnish study. If this lasts more than a week or two, or comes with snoring, pain, poor weight gain or great exhaustion in the family, talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: Does more food or formula make a baby sleep longer?
faq.answer: Probably not. In a study of 715 mothers of babies aged 6 to 12 months, those who ate or fed more during the day were less likely to feed at night, but not less likely to wake. There was also no difference in wakings between breast and formula at this age.

guides.title: Starting solids at 6 months: BLW vs purées
guides.description: Practical comparison of BLW (baby-led weaning) and traditional spoon-fed purées at 6 months: what AAP, WHO and ESPGHAN recommend, signs of readiness, choking risk, allergens, and how to combine both.

faq.question: Does BLW increase choking risk?
faq.answer: Comparative studies have not found a significant increase in true choking (airway obstruction) between babies on BLW and babies on purées, as long as families receive guidance on safe food shapes. The BLISS trial (New Zealand, 2017) and later reviews showed similar rates. What's often confused with choking is the gag reflex (a protective reflex of the throat), which is normal and very frequent during the first year. Real choking involves loss of color, no sound, and breathing difficulty — and demands an immediate first-aid maneuver.

faq.question: Can I start before 6 months if my baby 'seems interested'?
faq.answer: Current guidance from WHO, AAP and ESPGHAN is to start at 6 completed months — not earlier. Before 4 months, the digestive tract and kidneys aren't ready. Between 4 and 6 months, the AAP allows starting in specific cases (for example, on medical advice for poor weight gain on formula), but for healthy exclusively breastfed babies the reference is 6 months. Showing 'interest' in food (looking, opening the mouth) is common from 4 months on and isn't enough by itself — the baby also needs head control, ability to sit with little support, and loss of the tongue-thrust reflex.

faq.question: When should I introduce allergens like egg, peanut and fish?
faq.answer: The recommendation has flipped in the last decade. Today AAP, ESPGHAN and the NIAID guidelines recommend introducing major allergens (egg, peanut, fish, wheat, milk, soy, tree nuts, shellfish) around 6 months, alongside other foods — not later. The LEAP study (NEJM, 2015) showed that early peanut exposure in high-risk babies reduced the development of peanut allergy by about 80%. For babies with severe eczema or known egg allergy, the allergist may recommend evaluation before peanut — talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: Do I have to wait 3 days between new foods?
faq.answer: The classic '3-day rule' has weak evidence and has been relaxed in recent guidelines. What matters is to introduce each major allergen on its own the first few times (so you can spot a reaction), but offering several new foods in a week is safe and even encouraged for variety. Allergic reactions usually show up within 2 hours of the offer — that's the window to watch closely.

faq.question: Can I offer honey?
faq.answer: No. Honey is contraindicated before 12 months due to the risk of infant botulism (Clostridium botulinum). Also avoid cow's milk as a main drink before 1 year (small amounts in cooked food are tolerated), added sugar and added salt before 1 year, juice before 1 year (offer the whole fruit instead), and choking-shaped foods (whole grapes, popcorn, whole nuts, sliced hot dogs).

faq.question: How much milk should the baby keep drinking after 6 months?
faq.answer: Breast milk (or formula) remains the main source of nutrition until around 12 months. WHO recommends continuing breastfeeding to 2 years or beyond, alongside complementary food. In the first 2 to 3 months of solids, food is mostly exploration — offer it before or after a milk feed, without replacing it. By 8–9 months, food starts to take real caloric space, and milk naturally tapers off (but stays important).

guides.title: Breastfeeding in the first days: what to expect
guides.description: First-week breastfeeding guide: colostrum, milk coming in, latch, signs your baby is getting enough, and when to seek help.

faq.question: My milk hasn't come in yet — is my baby hungry?
faq.answer: Almost never. For the first 2–4 days, what comes out is colostrum — in small volumes (5–15 ml per feed on day 1), because a newborn's stomach is the size of a cherry. That volume is exactly what they need. The 'milk coming in' (lactogenesis II) usually happens between days 3 and 5, with volume increasing alongside.

faq.question: How often should the baby breastfeed in the first days?
faq.answer: On demand — typically 8 to 12 times in 24 hours, sometimes more. Newborns don't follow a schedule and may cluster feed every hour for stretches and sleep 3 hours at others. There's no minimum interval between feeds.

faq.question: How do I know my baby is getting enough?
faq.answer: Diapers and weight are the best indicators. From day 5 on, expect 6–8 wet diapers and at least 3–4 yellow stools per day. The baby should be back to birth weight by 10–14 days. An active baby at the breast who comes off on their own and stays calm between feeds is another good sign.

faq.question: Is pain during nursing normal?
faq.answer: Mild discomfort in the first few seconds can happen at the start, but pain that lasts the entire feed is not normal — it usually points to a poor latch. Get help from a lactation consultant or a milk bank. Cracks, bleeding, or throbbing pain between feeds need evaluation.

faq.question: Can I offer formula 'just to top up' in the first days?
faq.answer: Only with medical indication. Early formula supplementation without clinical need reduces the milk-production stimulus (which is demand-driven) and can compromise long-term breastfeeding. If you have real concerns about intake, talk to your pediatrician before supplementing on your own.

faq.question: When should I see a lactation consultant?
faq.answer: Whenever you have persistent pain, latch difficulties, suspected low supply, weight loss greater than 10% in the first days, or simply if something doesn't feel right. The earlier the help, the faster the resolution. In many countries, milk banks and IBCLC consultants offer support in the first weeks postpartum.

guides.title: Cluster feeding: why your baby wants to nurse all the time
guides.description: What cluster feeding is, why babies chain short feeds back-to-back (especially in the evening), at what ages it happens, and how to ride it out — without weaning, without supplementing on reflex.

faq.question: Is cluster feeding a sign my milk supply is low?
faq.answer: Almost always, no. Cluster feeding is a normal pattern of short back-to-back feeds, most common in the evening and during growth spurts. Babies do it to stimulate supply, for comfort, and because evening breast milk has more fat. If diapers (6 to 8 wet per day after day 5) and weight gain are on track, supply is fine — regardless of the 'empty breast' feeling.

faq.question: At what ages is cluster feeding most common?
faq.answer: In the first 2 to 3 weeks (establishing supply), around 3 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months and 6 months (classic growth spurts), and during illness, developmental leaps or after changes (vaccinations, travel, separation). Can pop up at any moment — typical duration 1 to 4 days in a row, rarely more.

faq.question: How long does a cluster feeding episode usually last?
faq.answer: An evening cluster typically lasts 2 to 4 hours in one night. A growth spurt with intense cluster feeding usually resolves in 24 to 72 hours — within a week the rhythm is back to baseline. If the pattern stretches past 5 to 7 days without returning to baseline, or if weight gain and diapers fall outside the expected range, it warrants evaluation.

faq.question: Should I supplement with formula during these stretches?
faq.answer: Not on reflex. Supplementing without clinical indication reduces stimulation at the breast precisely when the baby is signaling for supply to go up — and tends to start a cycle of less milk and more formula. When there is a real indication (weight loss outside the expected range, signs of dehydration, identified low supply), supplementation should be guided by a pediatrician or IBCLC lactation consultant, ideally with expressed breast milk and via cup, spoon, or supplemental nursing system.

faq.question: Do bottle-fed babies cluster feed too?
faq.answer: Yes, less intensely. Formula-fed babies also go through growth spurts and fussy evening phases, asking for the bottle every 1.5 to 2 hours instead of the usual spacing. The rule is the same: honor hunger when it comes, without forcing extra volume just to 'stretch' the interval. Formula digests more slowly, so cluster frequency tends to be lower than at the breast.

faq.question: How do I survive a cluster feeding night without losing my mind?
faq.answer: Accepting that the night will be hours back-to-back at the breast (not your fault) helps more than trying to 'break' the pattern. Use a comfortable chair or bed, keep water and a snack within reach, alternate sides as the baby leads, and split with your partner what doesn't need the breast (diaper change, holding between feeds, bath). The end of the cluster is usually followed by the longest stretch of sleep — so the night rarely ends up as rough as it feels in the middle of it.

guides.title: Developmental Leaps in Babies: What the Science Says
guides.description: Are developmental leaps real? What studies show about the week-by-week calendar, the link with sleep, what helps, and when to talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: Are developmental leaps real?
faq.answer: Partly. Babies do have phases of more crying, more holding and worse sleep, and new skills can affect sleep. What has little evidence is the idea of leaps in predictable weeks, the same for every baby. It comes from small studies, with 15 mothers in the original work and 18 babies in another study, with no large research confirming it as far as we could find.

faq.question: How long does a developmental leap last?
faq.answer: We found no well-established timeframe. In a study of 28 babies followed from 5 to 11 months, sleep got worse around the start of crawling while overall sleep kept improving across the period, but that doesn't set a duration for each baby. If things stay worse for more than two weeks, or come with other symptoms, it is worth talking to your pediatrician. That timeframe is our suggestion.

faq.question: Do developmental leaps disrupt sleep?
faq.answer: They can. Among 107 babies aged 5 to 8 months, those already crawling had more bedtime difficulties and more night wakings than those not yet crawling. In a study that measured sleep with a sensor, interruptions rose around the start of crawling. Both studies are small and don't prove it is the same for every baby.

faq.question: How can I tell a leap from an illness?
faq.answer: Look at the whole picture. More holding and worse sleep in a baby who is well, feeding, without fever and learning new things tend to be less worrying. Fever, pain, vomiting, refusing to feed, few wet diapers, limpness or losing something they already did should not be put down to a leap. In those cases, talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: Is it worth following a leap calendar?
faq.answer: It can be a comfort, but not a prediction. Since the evidence is limited, your baby doesn't have to be in crisis that week, and a calendar should not delay an appointment. To follow development, age milestones are a better reference: the CDC and the American Academy of Pediatrics use what at least 75% of children already do at that age.

guides.title: The first 30 days with a newborn: a survival guide
guides.description: What to expect in your baby's first month: sleep, feeding, diapers, the umbilical cord, crying, and your own recovery. A practical, no-panic guide to the fourth trimester.

faq.question: How many times does a newborn feed per day in the first month?
faq.answer: Usually 8 to 12 times in 24 hours — roughly every 2 to 3 hours, counting from the start of one feed to the start of the next. The interval is often similar at night. Babies fed on demand eat when they show hunger cues (rooting, hands to mouth, fussing), not by the clock.

faq.question: Is it normal for a newborn to sleep all day and stay awake at night?
faq.answer: Yes, it's very common in the first weeks. Your baby has no established circadian rhythm yet, so day and night get 'mixed up.' This usually starts sorting itself out around 6 to 8 weeks. It helps to expose your baby to natural light during the day and keep night feeds calm, with low light and little stimulation.

faq.question: When does the umbilical cord stump fall off?
faq.answer: Typically between 5 and 15 days of life, though it can take up to about 3 weeks, which is also normal. Keep the area clean and dry, let it air out, and fold the diaper down below the stump. See your pediatrician if there is redness on the surrounding skin, pus-like discharge, a strong odor, or bleeding that won't stop.

faq.question: How many wet diapers should a newborn have per day?
faq.answer: From around day 5, expect at least 6 well-soaked wet diapers a day plus several bowel movements. It's one of the best signs your baby is feeding enough. Fewer than that, very dark urine, or a very sleepy baby who won't wake to feed all warrant a check with your pediatrician.

faq.question: Can I have visitors in the first week?
faq.answer: You can, but on your own time and your own terms. You owe no one a visit. If you do host, ask everyone to wash their hands, keep away anyone with a cold or flu, and don't pass the baby from person to person. Protecting the mother's rest and the family's bonding comes before any social calendar.

faq.question: When should I seek urgent medical care in the first month?
faq.answer: Seek care immediately if your baby has a fever (100.4°F / 38°C or higher), is very floppy or hard to wake, refuses several feeds in a row, has trouble breathing, turns bluish or very yellow in the skin or lips, or if you simply feel something is wrong. In a newborn, any fever is an immediate evaluation.

guides.title: How Many Cans of Formula Does a Baby Go Through in a Month?
guides.description: How many cans of formula (400 g or 800 g) a baby uses per month, by age: the yield math, a 0–12 month chart, a calculator, and what it means for the budget — without ever becoming a bottle target.

faq.question: How many cans of formula does a baby go through in a month?
faq.answer: It depends on age and daily intake. The math is simple: a 400 g can yields about 2.8 to 3.1 liters of prepared formula (at the standard dilution of 1 level scoop per 30 ml of water — the powder adds volume to the mix). At peak intake — an exclusively formula-fed baby drinking 800 to 950 ml a day, between 1 and 5 months — that's around 8 to 10 cans of 400 g per month, or 4 to 5 of 800 g. Newborns use less (5 to 7 cans) and, after 6 months, intake falls as solids come in.

faq.question: How much formula does a 400 g can make?
faq.answer: About 2.8 to 3.1 liters of prepared formula. The math: every 30 ml of water takes 1 level scoop (4.3 to 4.7 g depending on the brand), and the powder adds volume — 30 ml of water + 1 scoop makes ~33 ml of formula. In total, 400 g of powder prepares 2,800 to 3,100 ml. An 800 g can makes double (5.6 to 6.2 liters). Your brand's real yield is on the label, in the preparation chart.

faq.question: How many days does a can of formula last?
faq.answer: Divide the yield by your baby's daily intake. Examples with a 400 g can (2.8 to 3.1 L): a 1-month-old drinking 700 ml/day → ~4 days; a 3-month-old drinking 900 ml/day → ~3 days; an 8-month-old drinking 500 ml/day → ~6 days. Important: once opened, the can must be used within the label's window — brands state 3 to 4 weeks, kept tightly closed in a dry place.

faq.question: Is the 800 g can better value than the 400 g one?
faq.answer: The price per gram of the 800 g can is almost always lower — compare price per kilo on the shelf tag, not the sticker price. The exception is low intake (a small top-up in combination feeding, or a baby near 1 year drinking little): if the opened can won't be finished within the label's window, the saving becomes waste.

faq.question: Can I dilute formula differently from the label to make the can last longer?
faq.answer: Never. The ratio (1 level scoop per 30 ml of water) is calculated to deliver the right nutrition and hydration. Watered-down formula undernourishes and can cause dangerous sodium imbalance; over-concentrated formula overloads the baby's kidneys. If cost is a struggle, bring it to the pediatrician as a problem to solve together — safe alternatives exist, and improvising on dilution is not one of them.

faq.question: My baby didn't finish what the chart predicted. Are they eating too little?
faq.answer: The cans chart is for planning purchases, not for measuring your baby. Intake varies with growth spurts, sleep, heat and plain appetite — some days more, some days less. The signs that all is well are different ones: weight gain on the curve, at least 6 well-soaked diapers a day (from the first week of life), and a baby content between feeds. If those three are fine, leftover formula is not a worry — and if the doubt persists, bring the question to the checkup instead of pushing volume.

guides.description: Recommended sleep hours from newborn to 2 years, based on the American Academy of Sleep Medicine, the National Sleep Foundation, and WHO.

faq.question: My baby sleeps less than the minimum of the range. Is something wrong?
faq.answer: It might be normal individual variation, or it might warrant a check. Look at three things: does the baby wake up rested and in a good mood? Are weight and height tracking on the growth chart? Can the baby focus and engage during play? If yes, you're likely fine. If they're chronically irritable, with dark circles under their eyes, or noticeably sleepy during the day, talk to your pediatrician.

faq.question: How much of that total should be nighttime sleep vs. naps?
faq.answer: It changes a lot with age. Newborns sleep in 2–4 hour blocks day and night, with no real distinction. Around 4 months, sleep starts consolidating at night. By 12 months, the typical pattern is 10–12 hours overnight + 2–3 hours of naps. By age 2, it's 11–12 hours overnight + one 1–2 hour nap.

faq.question: If a baby sleeps more than the upper end of the range, should I worry?
faq.answer: Usually not, but watch them. Healthy newborns can sleep up to 19 hours on some days. The flag is when sleep is so heavy the baby skips feeds, loses weight, or seems hard to rouse for a meal. That's when you call the pediatrician.

faq.question: Do fragmented nights (waking up several times) count toward the total?
faq.answer: Yes. The recommendations sum up all sleep across 24 hours, day and night. Waking up to feed in the early months is physiological and expected. Sleep quality matters too, but total quantity is the first signal to look at.

guides.description: Newborns: 5–15 ml per feed on days 1–2, 20–60 ml in week 1, 60–90 ml at 15 days and 60–120 ml near day 30. Day-by-day chart (0–30 days), 8–12 feeds and the signs your baby is getting enough.

faq.question: How many ml does a 15-day-old baby drink?
faq.answer: Around 15 days, a newborn takes on average 60 to 90 ml per feed, in 8 to 12 feeds across 24 hours — roughly 500 to 750 ml a day. At the breast you can't (and don't need to) measure: the reference is diapers (at least 5 to 6 well-soaked per day) and weight gain, since by this age the baby should have regained their birth weight.

faq.question: How many ml does a 20-day-old drink? And a 24-day-old?
faq.answer: Between 20 and 30 days the ranges merge into those of the full first month: 60 to 110 ml per feed, moving toward 60 to 120 ml near day 30, for a total of 600 to 850 ml a day in formula-fed babies. Exact days (20, 22, 24, 26...) don't change the math — what changes the amount is the baby's weight and that day's appetite, not the calendar date.

faq.question: How many ml does a newborn drink in the first days of life?
faq.answer: Much less than most people expect: 5 to 15 ml of colostrum per feed on days 1 and 2 (with formula, many newborns take 15 to 30 ml) — the stomach is still very small. Between day 3 and day 7 capacity grows fast and the volume rises to 20 to 60 ml per feed. That's why colostrum, produced in small amounts and highly concentrated, is enough in the first days.

faq.question: How do I know how many ml my baby gets at the breast?
faq.answer: You can't measure it — and you don't need to. In breastfeeding the reference isn't volume, it's feeding on demand: offer whenever your baby shows hunger cues (8 to 12 times or more in 24 hours during the first month) and confirm it's enough through external signs: at least 5 to 6 well-soaked diapers a day from day 4–5 on, regular stools, and weight gain on the growth curve followed by the pediatrician.

faq.question: My newborn sleeps a lot and skips feeds. Should I let them sleep?
faq.answer: Until the baby regains their birth weight (usually between day 10 and 14), the guidance is not to let much more than 3 to 4 hours pass without a feed — including overnight: wake gently, change the diaper, do skin-to-skin. Babies with jaundice, late preterm babies, or slow weight gain may need shorter intervals, set by the pediatrician. Once birth weight is back and gain is consistent, it's the pediatrician — at a visit, examining the baby — who clears longer stretches at night.

faq.question: How do I know my newborn is eating enough?
faq.answer: Three signs matter more than any chart: diapers (at least 5 to 6 well-soaked per day from day 4–5 of life), weight (losing up to 7 to 10% in the first days is expected, with birth weight regained by day 10–14) and behavior (a baby who settles after feeds and has calm alert periods). Fewer diapers than that, extreme sleepiness, or several refused feeds in a row: call the pediatrician without waiting for the routine visit.
